description:
I'm taking on NASA's Space Mission Design Game challenge, and building a game that lets you find out. You pick the destination, choose your spacecraft, build your crew and manage your budget. Then you live with the consequences: a long trip, tight supplies, risky landings and hard calls.
Everything in the game is grounded in real NASA mission data, so players learn how space missions work while they play. 48 hours to build something simple, fun and educational for anyone who has interest in it.
summary:
We developed Space Mission 101 , an interactive 3D browser-based aerospace engineering and flight simulation platform for the Space Mission Design Challenge. Users can explore a walkable 3D space agency headquarters, assemble modular multi-stage rockets and spacecraft with a live cutaway view, and launch across five progressive missions from Low Earth Orbit and Lunar landing to Mars surface operations, ISS docking, and a deep-space Jupiter probe complete with a T-5 audio-visual countdown and a fast ~15-second flight-to-debrief loop.
Space Mission 101 tackles the Space Mission Design Challenge through discovery-first systems engineering. Rather than spoiling design mistakes with pre-launch warning checklists, the simulator lets builders test their own trade-offs in thrust-to-weight ratio, propellant chemistry,  solar power limits and etc ... , After every launch, a post-flight debrief reveals the exact cause of any failure, the engineering fix, matching NASA Lessons Learned case studies, optimization tips, and a side-by-side comparison against real launch vehicles . 
This game can be seen as a learning opportunity through game for students of various age groups as well as for anyone who is interested in learning about Space Mission and Payload , also it can be extended using the available real data along with Machine Learning technique to use it as a prediction tool for future missions it can predict the output and also show the possible causes that may occur .
details:
What benefits does it have?
Most space engineering tools are either super complicated CAD software or simple text calculators that feel dry to use. Space Mission 101 puts everything into a browser-based 3D simulator that runs right away without installing anything. You can walk around a 3D space headquarters, swap rocket engines, fuel types, boosters, solar arrays, antennas, and science payloads, and see the rocket update right in front of you. Instead of waiting minutes for a flight to finish, the launch-to-result loop takes around 15 seconds with a big countdown display and voice audio. Best of all, it doesn't spoil mistakes before you launch. You test your design, see what happens in flight, and then get a clear breakdown of what failed, why the physics caused it, how to fix it, and how your rocket compares to real launchers like Falcon 9 or Saturn V.

What is the intended impact of the project?
The main goal is to help students, beginners, and anyone curious about space actually build intuition for how mission design works. When you pick a mission to Mars or Jupiter and watch your solar panels fail because sunlight drops off with distance, or your rocket fails to lift off because its thrust-to-weight ratio is below 1.02, the physics clicks in a way reading a textbook doesn't. By tying every failure and success back to real NASA Lessons Learned cases and historical missions, the project turns trial and error into a practical learning loop that makes aerospace engineering feel approachable and fun.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?
I built the application using TypeScript, React, and Tailwind CSS for the interface, and Three.js (WebGL) to render the 3D headquarters, rockets, spacecraft, and planetary environments procedurally without needing external 3D asset packs. For the launch countdown and sound effects, I used the browser's built-in Web Audio API and Web Speech API. The project is bundled with Vite and esbuild, which also allowed me to export it into a single standalone HTML file that runs offline, with campaign progress saved in browser local Storage. Development and testing were done on a standard laptop and web browser. I also used AI tools to assist with parts of the code, audio synthesis setup, organizing the NASA reference data, and generating the slide visuals (which are watermarked and acknowledged in the metadata).

How is your project creative?
Instead of giving players a checklist of green checkmarks before launch, I designed it around discovery first. We hid pre-launch warnings on purpose so you have to think through the engineering trade-offs yourself, launch your rocket, and learn from the outcome. Combining a walkable 3D space center, a cutaway rocket and spacecraft builder, a fast 15-second launch sequence with spoken countdown callouts, and a post-flight debrief anchored to real NASA incident reports and launcher benchmarks makes it feel both like a playable game and a real engineering lab. Packaging the whole 3D app into a single offline HTML file also makes it easy to share and run anywhere.

What factors did your team consider?
First, I thought a lot about pacing and readability. Earlier versions took too long between hitting launch and seeing the final result, and the HUD text was too heavy and cluttered, so I shortened the flight timeline, added automatic stage progression while keeping manual controls available, and cleaned up the typography so numbers and telemetry are easy to read at a glance. Second, I focused on realism versus accessibility—keeping real equations like the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, inverse-square solar flux, and communication link limits under the hood without overwhelming someone who is new to orbital mechanics. Finally, I considered portability and transparency, making sure it runs smoothly in a browser without a backend server and clearly disclosing where real NASA reference data and AI-assisted assets were used
